title: Same Tree
description: Two binary trees are identical iff their roots match in value AND their left and right subtrees are recursively identical. Straight structural recursion.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"So I need to determine if two binary trees `p` and `q` are 'the same' — meaning they have identical structure AND identical values at every corresponding position. If one tree has a node where the other has null at the same position, they're different even if all the values where both exist would match."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Are we comparing structure + values, or just values (e.g. ignoring missing children)? (Standard is structure + values.)
• Both empty trees → return true?
• Node shape — `{ val, left, right }` with `null` children?
• Should I return early on the first mismatch, or compare every node? (Early return is the standard, but it's worth confirming there's no 'count differences' variant.)
sections.why: The 'structure + values' framing is the easy thing to misread — some candidates compare values via in-order traversal and miss that `[1,2]` (left child only) and `[1,null,2]` (right child only) produce the same in-order [1,2] but are different trees. Confirming structure matters too — and that the algorithm must check shape, not just contents — locks in the right approach from the start.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious recursive solution — and the BFS alternative for stack safety.
sections.say:
"There's no slower naive here — the natural recursive solution is O(n) and visits each pair of corresponding nodes once. I'd describe it as: three base cases up front — both null → true, exactly one null → false, values differ → false — then recurse on (p.left, q.left) AND (p.right, q.right) with short-circuiting `&&`.

The iterative alternative uses parallel BFS or DFS: maintain a queue of (p_node, q_node) pairs. Pop a pair, apply the same three base-case checks, push the children pairs. Same O(n) time, O(w) or O(h) space depending on traversal order. Iterative version trades clarity for stack safety on deep trees."
sections.why: Calling out that there's no meaningful brute force — and offering the iterative variant as a stack-safety alternative — is the right framing. Interviewers want to see judgment about which tool fits; offering both options without padding shows you've thought about the tradeoff. The iterative version's value is purely stack safety, not asymptotic, and saying so demonstrates you don't conflate 'iterative' with 'faster.'

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to parallel recursion?
sections.say:
"The property to check is defined recursively over both trees simultaneously: two trees are 'same' iff their roots match AND their corresponding subtrees (both lefts, both rights) are 'same.' That's the textbook signature of parallel structural recursion — walk two trees in lockstep, making the same check at every paired position. Not a single-tree recursion that returns something interesting; a pair-of-trees recursion where the result is just true/false.

The three base cases come from the cartesian product of (p exists or not) × (q exists or not): both missing is fine (true), one missing while the other isn't is mismatch (false), both present requires value match plus recursion. That cartesian exhaustion is what makes the algorithm complete — every position in either tree is accounted for.

Parallel recursion (or parallel BFS) is the same family that shows up in Symmetric Tree, Mirror of a Tree, Subtree Check — anytime you're comparing two tree structures position-by-position."
sections.why: Naming 'parallel recursion' — and explaining the three base cases come from the cartesian product of nullable positions — is the derivation. 'Use recursion' alone is too vague; 'parallel recursion because we're walking two trees in lockstep' is specific. The connection to Symmetric Tree and Subtree Check proves you see the family, which is the kind of pattern-level understanding interviewers grade on.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — fully identical, value mismatch, and shape mismatch (the in-order-trap case).

examples.note: Fully identical — algorithm walks both trees in lockstep, all checks pass.
examples.trace:
isSame(1, 1): both non-null, vals match (1===1). recurse:
  isSame(2, 2): both non-null, vals match. recurse:
    isSame(null, null): both null → true
    isSame(null, null): both null → true
    → true && true = true
  isSame(3, 3): both non-null, vals match. recurse:
    isSame(null, null): true
    isSame(null, null): true
    → true
  → true && true = true
return true

examples.note: Right child value differs — short-circuit return on mismatch.
examples.trace:
isSame(1, 1): vals match. recurse:
  isSame(2, 2): vals match. recurse on children, all null → true
  isSame(3, 4): vals differ (3 !== 4) → return false
  → true && false = false
return false

examples.note: Shape mismatch — in-order traversal would give [1,2] for both, but structures differ. This is THE in-order-trap case.
examples.trace:
isSame(p_root_1, q_root_1): vals match (1===1). recurse:
  isSame(p.left=2, q.left=null): exactly one null → return false
  → false && (right recursion not evaluated due to short-circuit)
return false

sections.why: The third trace is the load-bearing one — it exposes the in-order trap. A candidate who solves this with 'flatten both trees in-order and compare arrays' would return TRUE here, because both trees produce in-order [1, 2]. The parallel-recursion approach correctly returns false at the (left, null) mismatch. Walking through this trace out loud is what convinces an interviewer you understand WHY shape matters separately from values.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Both null → both-null base case returns true. ✓
• One null, one non-null root → exactly-one-null base case returns false. ✓
• Single node, same value → vals match, both children recursions return true (both null on both sides). ✓
• Single node, different values → vals-differ base case returns false. ✓
• Trees with identical in-order but different shapes (e.g. [1,2] vs [1,null,2]) → the in-order trap. Parallel recursion catches it via the exactly-one-null check; in-order-then-compare would miss it.
• All-same values (e.g. [1,1,1] vs [1,1,1]) → walks both fully, returns true.
• One tree huge, other tiny — first mismatch (likely an exactly-one-null in the recursion) short-circuits to false; we don't walk the whole large tree.
• Left-skewed (degenerate to linked list) → recursion depth = n, stack-overflow risk on adversarial input.
• Floating-point values like NaN — `NaN !== NaN` so trees with NaN at corresponding positions would compare as different. Worth flagging if values are floats."
sections.why: The in-order trap callout is the senior signal — most interview problems don't have a 'tempting wrong solution' to call out, and this one does. The NaN edge is bonus depth for floats — most candidates never think about it, but `Number.isNaN(v) && Number.isNaN(u)` is the careful comparison if NaN is in scope. Either flagging earns you 'thinks about edges' credit.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(min(|p|, |q|)) in the early-return case (we stop at the first mismatch), and O(n) where n = max tree size in the full-match case. The standard answer is O(n) because the worst case is two identical trees that require visiting every node pair.

Space is O(h) for the recursion stack — log n balanced, n worst case skewed. Iterative parallel BFS would be O(w) instead.

The short-circuit via `&&` is a real performance win when trees mismatch early — recursion doesn't even enter the right subtree once the left disagrees. Worth using `&&` rather than evaluating both and AND-ing the results.

If you wanted to extend this to 'is `subRoot` a subtree of `root`' (LeetCode 572), you'd call `isSameTree` from every node of `root`: at each `n` in `root`, check if `isSameTree(n, subRoot)`. That's O(m·n) naively; can be made O(m+n) with serialization + KMP, but the natural recursive version reuses this function as a primitive."
sections.why: Naming early-return as O(min) and full-match as O(n) shows you've thought about the actual cost profile, not just the worst case. The Subtree Check extension is LeetCode 572 and uses `isSameTree` as a building block — calling that out proves you see this as a primitive in the tree-comparison family, not just a one-off question. That's the kind of compositional thinking that distinguishes pattern fluency.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the structural same-tree check. The trace simulates the recursion with an explicit work-list of (p,q) node pairs; each pair must pass the three base cases before its children are queued.
trace: const { p: pArr, q: qArr } = input;
if (!arr || arr.length === 0 || arr[0] == null) return null;
const root = { val: arr[0], left: null, right: null };
if (i < arr.length && arr[i] != null) { node.left = { val: arr[i], left: null, right: null }; q.push(node.left); }
if (i < arr.length && arr[i] != null) { node.right = { val: arr[i], left: null, right: null }; q.push(node.right); }
yield { line: 1, label: `enter isSameTree — p=${JSON.stringify(pArr)}, q=${JSON.stringify(qArr)}`, state: { pShape: pArr, qShape: qArr } };
yield { line: 1, label: `compare ${aStr} vs ${bStr}`, state: { pShape: pArr, qShape: qArr, a: a ? a.val : null, b: b ? b.val : null } };
yield { line: 2, label: 'both null → true (this pair OK, continue)', state: { pShape: pArr, qShape: qArr } };
yield { line: 3, label: `exactly one null (${aStr} vs ${bStr}) → return false`, state: { pShape: pArr, qShape: qArr, result } };
yield { line: 4, label: `values differ (${a.val} !== ${b.val}) → return false`, state: { pShape: pArr, qShape: qArr, result } };
yield { line: 5, label: `values match (${a.val} === ${b.val}) — queue children pairs`, state: { pShape: pArr, qShape: qArr, current: a.val } };
yield { line: 5, label: `done — return ${result}`, state: { pShape: pArr, qShape: qArr, returns: result } };

notes: Three base cases in order: both null → true, exactly one null → false, values differ → false.
Short-circuit `&&` so the right subtree isn't walked once the left disagrees.
Space is O(h), the height of the tree — O(n) worst case for a skewed tree, O(log n) for balanced.

alternates.label: Iterative paired queue (BFS)
alternates.when: Reach for this when the trees could be adversarially deep (skewed to ~10k+ nodes in JS) and you want to avoid call-stack overflow. Applies identical base-case logic per pair; trades O(h) recursion for O(w) queue space.
notes: Queue holds PAIRS of corresponding nodes — the same three base-case checks apply per pair, just inside a loop instead of recursive calls.
Null pairs are a legitimate entry in the queue (both null → continue, one null → false) so you never need to guard before pushing children.
Space is O(w) where w is the max level width across both trees; for balanced trees that is ~n/2, potentially heavier than recursion's O(log n) average.

questions.q: What is the correct base case when BOTH p and q are null?
options: Return false — there is nothing to compare
Return true — two empty subtrees are identical
Return true only if both parent nodes had the same value; otherwise false
Skip this pair and continue with the next recursive call without returning
questions.explain: Two missing subtrees are trivially the same shape.

questions.q: What if exactly one of p or q is null?
options: Treat the missing node as a fresh node with the same val as its sibling and continue
Return true
Return false — the structures differ
Recurse on the non-null one

questions.q: If you check `p.val !== q.val` BEFORE the null checks, what bug occurs?
options: Same output, just slightly slower
Throws TypeError — `p.val` crashes when p is null
Returns wrong answer on identical trees
Always returns false
questions.explain: `p.val` throws TypeError if p is null — must guard with both-null and one-null checks first. Order matters.

questions.q: Why use `&&` between the two recursive calls?
options: `&` would coerce the boolean returns to integers and break the recursion's truthiness
Both subtrees must match; `&&` also short-circuits when the left disagrees
`&&` evaluates the right recursion first, which matches the post-order semantics
Replacing it with `,` (comma operator) would evaluate only the right side and miss left mismatches

questions.q: Trees p=[1,2] (left child only) and q=[1,null,2] (right child only) have the same in-order traversal [1,2]. Are they the same tree?
options: Yes — identical in-order means identical tree
No — same values but different structure; the exactly-one-null check catches the mismatch
Yes — values are all that matter
Cannot be determined
questions.explain: Same-tree requires matching STRUCTURE plus values; comparing flattened in-order arrays misses shape differences, which is why parallel recursion is the correct approach.

questions.q: Can you solve Same Tree iteratively, and how?
options: No — it must be recursive
Yes — a queue (or stack) of PAIRED (p-node, q-node) tuples; pop a pair, run the same base-case checks, push the children pairs
Yes, but only with a priority queue
Yes, by hashing both trees to strings — the only way
questions.explain: The iterative form walks both trees in lockstep via a worklist of paired nodes, applying the identical base-case logic per pair.

questions.q: Tightest time complexity, given early-exit on the first mismatch?
options: O(min(n, m)) — you can't compare more pairs than the smaller tree has nodes (worst case still O(n) for identical trees)
O(log n)
questions.explain: Comparison stops at the first disagreement, bounded by the smaller tree; for two identical trees you must visit every node, so worst case is O(n).

questions.q: Why must the both-null and one-null base cases come BEFORE recursing into children?
options: For readability only
Recursing into children of a null node would dereference null.left/null.right and throw
It changes the time complexity
Children must be sorted first
questions.explain: The null guards stop the descent; without checking null first, the recursive call would access properties of a null node and crash.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the recursive same-tree check.

blanks.hint: either one alone null means mismatch

exercises.prompt: Structural recursion — both arguments must pair the SAME side from p and q. Blank the recursive args.

blanks.hint: pair p's left with q's left
pair p's right with q's right

L3.prompt: Write `isSameTree(p, q)` returning true iff two binary trees are structurally and value-equal. Log `isSameTree(a, b)` then `isSameTree(a, c)` where `c` differs in one node.
hints: Base cases first: both null → true, exactly one null → false.
Then check values, then recurse on both children with &&.
